newsitem.title: THAILAND: Watchdog worried about Burma refugees in Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Watchdog worried about Burma refugees in Thailand.

text.p: More than 100,000 Burmese refugees in Thailand are suffering because of Bangkok's policy of putting economic interests ahead of humanitarian concerns, the U.S. Committee for Refugees said on Wednesday.
"Thailand has been a generous nation in terms of refugee hosting for the past few years," said Hiram Ruiz, Asia policy analyst for USCR.

"Now Thailand sees new refugees as something that should only be a short-term phenomenon. Refugees are fleeing fighting in Burma, but they are told once fighting finishes they should return," he told a news conference.
Ruiz made the comments after a trip to the border and to Burma to evaluate the situation of Burmese refugees currently living in camps in Thailand.
"Refugees should not be obliged to return home until the basic reasons that caused them to flee have changed," he told reporters. "This has not been the case in Burma."
Thailand was accused earlier this year of forcibly repatriating some of the refugees who crossed into the country after fleeing fighting in Burma.
Bangkok denied the charges but says it only accepts unarmed Burmese into the refugee camps.
Ruiz said the USCR was concerned about the safety of the refugees in camps, especially those near the border, because of repeated attacks by Burmese troops and rival Karen factions.

"We have been concerned about the safety of the refugees in the camps. There have been many attacks on the refugee camps during 1996 and 1997 and there are threats that more attacks will take place," he said.
Ruiz also said Thailand has been putting newly arrived refugees from Burma in a "desperate situation" under poor conditions -- possibly to convince them to leave sooner.
In a news release, the USCR accused the Thai government of focusing on economic concerns at the refugees' expense.

"Recently, Thai economic interests in Burma have expanded markedly. To smooth the way for development of those economic interests, the Thai government, like others in the region, has sought to improve its relations with SLORC," it said, referring to Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council.
It said Thai authorities along the border have yielded to pressure by the SLORC to return the refugees and not allow new ones to enter Thailand.
"Their primary motivation is said to be their desire to promote Thai business intersts in Burma," it said.
The SLORC has been accused by human rights organisations and Western governments of human rights abuses.
Most of the refugees who have fled to Thailand and other neighbouring countries say they did so to escape forced portering, arbitrary arrests and forced labour in Burma.
